In multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (MADRL), communication protocols can be learned rather than predefined, alongside agents' value functions and policies. However, learning effective communication remains challenging in environments that are stochastic, continuous, or multi-task. This thesis addresses these challenges with the aim of improving learning stability, learning efficiency, and task performance through learnable and adaptive communication.\\n\\nFirst, we survey the literature on MADRL with communication and propose a classification framework of nine dimensions that capture key aspects of communication design and learning. The framework provides a structured basis for analyzing, comparing, and developing communication methods.\\n\\nSecond, we study the Communicating Critics and Decentralized Actors (CCDA) setting, in which critics exchange messages during training while actors act without communication at execution. Under stated assumptions on ideal and noisy communication, we show that the variance of policy gradients under communicating critics is equal to or greater than that obtained with a centralized critic that has access to the complete joint information. To mitigate this variance, we derive a message-dependent baseline, characterize its variance-minimizing form, and propose a complementary regularization technique. Experiments show reduced gradient variance and improved learning performance.\\n\\nThird, we propose Communication with Factorized Policy Gradients (CFPG) for continuous control. In multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (MADRL), communication protocols can be learned rather than predefined, alongside agents' value functions and policies. However, learning effective communication remains challenging in environments that are stochastic, continuous, or multi-task. This thesis addresses these challenges with the aim of improving learning stability, learning efficiency, and task performance through learnable and adaptive communication.\\n\\nFirst, we survey the literature on MADRL with communication and propose a classification framework of nine dimensions that capture key aspects of communication design and learning. The framework provides a structured basis for analyzing, comparing, and developing communication methods.\\n\\nSecond, we study the Communicating Critics and Decentralized Actors (CCDA) setting, in which critics exchange messages during training while actors act without communication at execution. Under stated assumptions on ideal and noisy communication, we show that the variance of policy gradients under communicating critics is equal to or greater than that obtained with a centralized critic that has access to the complete joint information. To mitigate this variance, we derive a message-dependent baseline, characterize its variance-minimizing form, and propose a complementary regularization technique. Experiments show reduced gradient variance and improved learning performance.\\n\\nThird, we propose Communication with Factorized Policy Gradients (CFPG) for continuous control. CFPG uses centralized but factorized value functions to distinguish the contribution of each communicating agent, and propagates gradients through both policies and message encoders so that communication and action selection are learned jointly. Experiments in continuous-control benchmarks show improved performance and faster learning relative to the evaluated baselines.\\n\\nFinally, we introduce Multi-task Communication Skills (MCS), a Transformer-based method that enables agents to learn and perform multiple tasks with a single shared communication protocol. The protocol accommodates varying numbers of agents as well as heterogeneous observation and action spaces by encoding task-specific observations into a shared message space, limiting unnecessary communication, and aggregating received messages. An additional learning objective encourages messages to carry information about the senders' actions.\\n\\nTogether, these contributions provide theoretical insights and practical methods for learning communication in cooperative MADRL. Evaluations on simulated benchmarks demonstrate improvements in learning stability, efficiency, or task performance relative to the evaluated baselines, with the magnitude of improvement varying across tasks.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.33540/3739\"}, {\"DOI\": \"10.58837/chula.the.2019.162\", \"title\": [\"Path exploration with random network distillation on multi-agent reinforcement learning\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Intrinsic motivation is one of the potential candidates to help improve performance of reinforcement learning algorithm in complex environments. The method enhances exploration capability without explicitly told by the creator and works on any environment. This is suitable in the case of multi-agent reinforcement learning where the environment complexity is more than usual. The research presents an exploration model using intrinsic motivation built from the random network distillation algorithm to improve the performance of multi-agent reinforcement learning and compare with the benchmark in different scenarios. The concept of clipping ratio is introduced to enforces the limit on optimization magnitude. Based on the extrinsic reward, the limit in the form of clipping ratio helps truncate the excessive magnitude that may cause instability to the optimization. The experiments were carried out on two different multi-agent architectures: 1) Individual Intrinsic Motivation Architecture, and 2) Centralized Intrinsic Motivation Architecture. The experimental results showed that in case of very complex environments, Centralized Intrinsic Motivation Architecture accompanied with a small clipping ratio could gain an increase in performance.
